title: Type Guards & Declaration Merging
description: User-defined type guards, assertion functions, module augmentation, and interface merging.

challenges.title: User-defined type guards
challenges.whyMatters: User-defined type guards are how you tell TypeScript what your runtime check means for the type system — without them, narrowing stays as unknown even when you've validated the shape.
hints: value is Config is a type predicate — it tells TypeScript to narrow value to Config in the true branch of callers

choices.label: It means the function always returns true for Config values
It is a type predicate — if the function returns true, TypeScript narrows value to Config at the call site
It is equivalent to a type assertion (value as Config)
It throws if value is not a Config

challenges.title: Assertion functions
challenges.whyMatters: Assertion functions are used in config validation and startup checks — call once at boot, and TypeScript narrows the type for the rest of the function without requiring an if statement.
hints: asserts narrows permanently after the call — no if/else needed

choices.label: val is still unknown — TypeScript doesn't trust assertion functions
val is string — the asserts return type tells TypeScript that if the function returns (doesn't throw), the value is narrowed
val is string | unknown — the assertion adds a type, not replaces
Compile error — you cannot call toUpperCase on unknown

challenges.title: Write type guards for a union
challenges.description:
Given these types:

  type Circle = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number }
  type Rectangle = { kind: 'rectangle'; width: number; height: number }
  type Triangle = { kind: 'triangle'; base: number; height: number }
  type Shape = Circle | Rectangle | Triangle

Write:
- `isCircle(s: unknown): s is Circle` — type guard
- `isRectangle(s: unknown): s is Rectangle` — type guard
- `area(shape: Shape): number` — returns area for each shape
  - circle: π * r²
  - rectangle: width * height
  - triangle: 0.5 * base * height
- `assertShape(val: unknown): asserts val is Shape` — throws if val is not a valid Shape
challenges.whyMatters: Shape-style discriminated unions appear in typed event systems, message queues, and command parsers. Type guards and assertion functions are how you safely enter those systems.
hints: Check that s is a non-null object first, then check the kind discriminant — casting to any is one safe way to access the property before the type is narrowed
area: switch on shape.kind — TypeScript narrows each case
assertShape: check that val has a valid kind property

challenges.title: Declaration merging — interfaces
challenges.whyMatters: Declaration merging is how you extend third-party types without forking them — adding fields to Express Request, augmenting process.env types, extending library interfaces.
hints: TypeScript merges multiple declarations of the same interface into one combined type

choices.label: Compile error — you cannot declare the same interface twice
The second declaration overwrites the first
Both declarations are merged — Config has both host and port, so both are required
The two declarations create a union type

challenges.title: Module augmentation
challenges.description:
Augment the `process.env` type to add typed fields for your app's required env vars.

In `solution.ts`, use module augmentation to add these to `NodeJS.ProcessEnv`:
- `APP_ENV?: string`
- `LOG_LEVEL?: string`
- `PORT?: string`
- `DB_URL?: string`

Then write a function `loadAppEnv(): { appEnv: string; logLevel: string; port: number; dbUrl: string }` that reads these fields with defaults:
- APP_ENV defaults to `'development'`
- LOG_LEVEL defaults to `'info'`
- PORT defaults to `3000` (parse as int)
- DB_URL throws if missing: `'Missing DB_URL'`
challenges.whyMatters: Augmenting ProcessEnv gives you autocomplete and type checking on process.env — one of the most impactful quick wins in any Node.js production codebase.
hints: Module augmentation for global Node types requires nesting: declare global, then a NodeJS namespace, then the ProcessEnv interface — add your fields with optional markers and string types
export {} at the bottom makes the file a module (required for global augmentation)
Parse PORT as an integer using base 10 — fall back to the string '3000' before parsing if the env var is not set

challenges.title: Narrowing with in and instanceof
challenges.whyMatters: Knowing which narrowing tool fits which situation prevents unnecessary type casts and keeps code readable.
hints: 'in' narrows plain objects by property; 'instanceof' narrows class instances

choices.label: Use 'in' for the discriminated union (check 'type'); use instanceof for the class hierarchy
Use the 'type' property directly for the union; use instanceof NetworkError for the class

challenges.title: Write assertion functions for startup validation
challenges.description:
Write a startup validation system using assertion functions:

  interface AppConfig { host: string; port: number; workers: number; logLevel: 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error' }

Write:
- `assertDefined<T>(val: T | undefined | null, name: string): asserts val is T` — generic assertion
- `assertPort(val: unknown): asserts val is number` — must be integer 1–65535
- `assertLogLevel(val: unknown): asserts val is AppConfig['logLevel']` — must be valid log level
- `assertConfig(raw: unknown): asserts raw is AppConfig` — validates the full shape using the above

All throw descriptive errors on failure.
challenges.whyMatters: Assertion functions at startup are the most ergonomic way to validate config — call once, then use the config everywhere with full type safety for the rest of the process lifetime.
hints: asserts val is T means: if this function returns (doesn't throw), val is T
assertConfig: cast to Record<string, unknown>, then call assertDefined, assertPort etc. on each field
A valid port must be an integer and fall within the valid port range — check all three conditions and throw a descriptive error if any fails
